Resource-Aware Agentic AI

# On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents

Aaron Wang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work done during an internship at AWS Agentic
AI. Affiliation: University of Illinois at Chicago    Neelabh
Madan¹¹footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: New York University    Vlad Sobal
Affiliation: AWS    Matthew Trager Affiliation: AWS    Michael Kleinman
Affiliation: AWS    Elman Mansimov Affiliation: AWS    Wei Xia
Affiliation: AWS    Stefano Soatto Affiliation: AWS

August 2026

###### Abstract

We study whether small LLM agents can operate effectively under explicit
wall-clock time budgets by both respecting the allocated runtime and
using available time productively. We evaluate Qwen3.6-27B on five
competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Qwen3-4B on Zork I (Jericho), two
agentic benchmarks where additional computational time can meaningfully
improve performance. In the simplest setting, where the budget is stated
only in the prompt, agents fail to translate the stated budget into
controlled use of time. These failures arise from gaps in time
awareness, since the harness provides no timing feedback, but also
because they cannot reliably anticipate the duration of actions, and do
not have a learned mapping from available time to an appropriate
strategy. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions:
harness-based mechanisms that expose timing information and enforce
deadlines, and reinforcement learning with budget-aware rewards.
Injecting timing information through the harness substantially improves
budget adherence for Qwen3.6-27B without measurable loss in performance,
while enforcement hooks tighten adherence further. RL with GRPO achieves
near-perfect budget adherence on Zork I and generalizes to held-out
budgets not seen during training, but does not improve task performance
over the untrained harness on MLE-Bench. Once agents are made to respect
the budget, they still fail to use additional time to improve task
performance. RL-trained policies learn when to stop but often fill extra
time with repeated actions, and GRPO training on multiple budgets tends
to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget. Our
results reveal a gap between time adherence and productive time
allocation, which remains a central challenge for budget-conditioned
agents.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: (Left two) Mean quality (leaderboard percentile) against mean
wall-clock time used by Qwen3.6-27B on MLE-Bench, with the budget stated
in the prompt (left) and with the enforcement harness added (right).
Color gives the stated budget and dashed lines mark the budget values.
(Right two) Mid-episode time estimation on 15-minute MLE-Bench tasks.
The agent is asked how long it has been working and how long the run
will take in total, and its answer is plotted against the true value,
with the dashed diagonal marking a perfect estimate. Open markers have a
clock in context, filled markers do not.

As AI agents take on complex, long-horizon tasks involving planning,
tool use, and iterative refinement, how long they spend on a task
becomes an important dimension of their behavior, alongside the quality
of the final solution. Agents should be able to operate effectively
under explicit wall-clock time budgets for two reasons. First, agents
face _external constraints_. A user should be able to control how long a
task takes end to end, and an agent embedded in a larger system must
meet deadlines to coordinate with other components. Second, for many
tasks _time is aligned with quality_. In search-heavy problems such as
ML engineering, more time allows an agent to explore more architectures,
hyperparameters, or candidate solutions, so making agents as fast as
possible is not the goal. At the same time, users differ in how they
weigh solution quality against time, and a time budget is how a user
expresses that trade-off.

We require two things from an agent operating under a budget, which we
call _adherence_ and _productive use_. Adherence means the agent returns
a solution within the allocated time; a harness can force this with a
hard interrupt, so that the agent works to the deadline itself.
Productive use means the agent spends that time well, using additional
budget to improve the solution rather than stopping early or padding its
runtime with unnecessary actions. A concrete test is whether task
performance improves as the budget increases. If the agent achieves the
same quality under a tight budget as under a generous one, the
additional time is not being converted into a better solution. Much of
these tasks are also dominated by tool call latencies, and we test how
well the model is able to take in both the latencies and its generation
time in order to stay in budget.

Current agents fail at adherence even in the simplest setting, where the
budget is stated in the prompt and the harness gives no feedback on
elapsed time. On MLE-Bench, Qwen3.6-27B does not use the allocated time
effectively
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents"),
left;
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).
Qwen3.6-27B runs for roughly ten minutes regardless of the stated
budget, overrunning an 8-minute budget while using a small fraction of a
60-minute budget.

| Model       | Budget | On time   | Elapsed                         | Quality         |
| ----------- | ------ | --------- | ------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Qwen3.6-27B | 8 min  | $`35\%`$  | $`12.9`$ $`\pm 12.6`$           | $`50.3\pm 2.9`$ |
|             | 15 min | $`83\%`$  | $`\phantom{0}9.7`$ $`\pm 10.6`$ | $`43.1\pm 8.6`$ |
|             | 60 min | $`100\%`$ | $`10.5`$ $`\pm 6.3`$            | $`54.8\pm 7.2`$ |
|             | none   | –         | $`12.2`$ $`\pm 11.4`$           | $`53.5\pm 7.8`$ |

These failures reflect concrete gaps in what the model can observe and
predict about time. Nothing in the model’s context indicates elapsed
wall-clock time, and token count is a poor proxy since it depends on
hardware and inference configuration. Probing the models directly
confirms this. Asked mid-episode how long it has been working, Qwen3.6
27b misjudges its own elapsed time by a large amount on a 15-minute task
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents"),
right;
Table [9](#Sx2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents"),
Appendix). Agents also cannot reliably predict how long their actions
will take, which matters most for long-running tool calls such as
training jobs, and even with a clock in context, forecasts of the run’s
remaining and total duration stay far off. We hypothesize that even an
agent with perfect timing information must still learn to map available
time to an appropriate plan.

We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based
and learning-based. _Harness-based_ interventions close the
observational gaps. A per-action clock and periodic reminders report the
remaining budget and the time cost of each action, and an enforcement
mode optionally holds the deadline by clamping or refusing over-long
commands. _Learning-based_ interventions target the planning gap. We
also explore reinforcement learning (GRPO) against budget-aware rewards
as a preliminary step toward internalizing the time–quality trade-off
directly. We evaluate on two agentic settings where additional time can
meaningfully improve outcomes, five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and
Zork I (Jericho), which differ in action structure, feedback density,
and how time converts into quality. We select a small number of tasks
where different budgets should favor different strategies, and analyze
failure modes in detail.

In this work, we separate the problem of time budgeting into adherence
and productive use, two parts of very different difficulty. We show that
_adherence_ is largely solvable in our settings. The harness brings
Qwen3.6-27B from $`161\%`$ of budget to on-budget with no measurable
loss in quality (between the runs with and without the harness), and RL
yields near-exact adherence on Zork I that generalizes to held-out
budgets, though training is less effective on MLE-Bench, where the
search space is much larger. _Productive use_, however, is much harder.
We show that agents that stay on time do not convert additional time
into better outcomes, and the RL policy that learns when to stop fills
extra time with actions that do not produce better task results.

## 2 Related Work

##### Budget-awareness and time-aware test-time scaling.

Lin et al. \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] formalize budget-awareness as progressive
interval estimation, where the agent predicts upper and lower bounds on
remaining budget at each step, and find that frontier agents are
consistently over-optimistic about how much budget remains. Their SFT+RL
training improves early-stop behavior, but precise calibration remains
difficult. Our work focuses on wall-clock time rather than token
budgets, and studies the progression from prompting through harness
enforcement to RL rather than a single training method. Li et
al. \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] propose a training-free Budget-Aware Value Tree
Search that shifts from exploration to exploitation as budget depletes,
and McCleary and Ghawaly \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] measure how search depth,
retrieval strategy, and completion budget affect accuracy under fixed
constraints. Both operate at the token or tool-call level. We study
wall-clock time, whose stochastic action durations token counting cannot
capture.

Snell et al. \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] show that a compute-optimal test-time
scaling strategy can outperform a $`14\times`$ larger model, but assume
an unlimited budget. Ma et al. \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] redefine test-time
scaling in wall-clock terms with the Timely-Eval benchmark and a
Timely-RL training method, and find that existing models fail to adapt
reasoning to time budgets. Where Ma et al. focus on a single RL
intervention, we compare prompting, harness enforcement, and RL as a
progression. Paglieri et al. \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] use SFT and RL to teach
agents when planning is worthwhile. We study how the entire strategy
should adapt to a time budget, and find that RL learns when to stop but
not what to do differently with more time.

##### Budgeted and constrained reinforcement learning.

Constrained Markov Decision Processes \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] formalize
reward maximization subject to cost constraints. Carrara et
al. \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] extend this to Budgeted MDPs, conditioning a
single policy on the budget so it solves the CMDP for any budget level
without retraining, an idea our RL stage adopts. Our cost signal,
wall-clock time, is stochastic and unpredictable, while classical BMDPs
assume known cost functions of state-action pairs. McMahan and
Zhu \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] require that the budget never be violated at any
point in time, closer to our setting since an agent that overruns at
step $`t`$ cannot undo it at $`t+1`$. Their result that Markovian
policies are insufficient under anytime constraints informs our choice
to inject remaining budget into the agent’s context.
Achille \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] argues that time is the critical quantity
to optimize when scaling reasoning models, and warns of a failure mode
in which reward-driven models brute-force solutions without acquiring
transferable strategies. Our RL-trained policy’s
memorized-prefix-plus-no-ops behavior matches this failure mode.

##### Reinforcement learning for LLMs.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) \[[11](#bib.bib11)\],
introduced for DeepSeek-Math and used for
DeepSeek-R1 \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], samples a group of rollouts per task
and normalizes rewards within the group, avoiding a separate critic
network. We adopt GRPO because this normalization handles the
multi-modal reward distribution produced by training across several
budget levels at once.

## 3 Setup

### 3.1 Datasets

We evaluate time-budgeted agent behavior in two environments: machine
learning engineering with MLE-Bench, and text-based games with Jericho
Zork. We chose both because task performance scales meaningfully with
wall-clock time, they admit multiple valid strategies at different
budget levels, and they give graded scores for partially completed work.

##### MLE-Bench Lite.

MLE-Bench \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] evaluates agents on end-to-end machine
learning tasks derived from Kaggle competitions. We use MLE-Bench Lite,
a 22-competition subset, and select 5 tasks from it based on two
criteria. The task must admit qualitatively different strategies at
different time scales (e.g. a quick baseline versus iterative feature
engineering), and preliminary runs must show non-trivial score variance
across time budgets ranging from 10 to 25 minutes. Each task requires
the agent to inspect data, develop and execute modeling code, iterate on
experiments, and produce a valid submission. The environment is well
suited for studying time-aware agents because additional wall-clock time
enables different activities. A short budget may suffice for a single
baseline model, while a longer budget allows time for data analysis,
feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and longer
training runs. We use a five-competition subset of MLE-Bench Lite,
namely dog-breed identification and dogs-vs-cats (image classification),
leaf classification (species classification from extracted leaf-image
features), spooky-author identification (text classification), and
NOMAD 2018 transparent-conductor prediction (tabular regression).

We use Qwen3.6-27B \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] as the underlying language
model, run through the OpenCode agentic harness. For RL training, we use
an internal tool to obtain TITO (Training In, Training Out) formatted
data from agent rollouts, converting trajectories into training samples
for GRPO. We vary the wall-clock budget and measure how the agent’s
trajectory and final task performance change as a function of available
time.

##### Jericho (Zork I).

Jericho \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] is an interactive-fiction environment in
which an agent interacts with a text-based game through natural-language
actions. We use zork1 for all experiments. At each step the model
observes the current game state, generates an action, and receives the
resulting observation. Additional time translates directly into more
exploration steps, and performance scales with how much of the world map
the agent discovers and how many puzzles it solves along the way.

For evaluations we use Qwen3-4B \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], Qwen3.5-9B and
Qwen3.8-27B \[[16](#bib.bib16)\] in a lightweight agentic loop with
thinking mode off. The model repeatedly receives the observation,
generates the next action, and observes the result until the trajectory
terminates or the time budget is exhausted. We define the task reward,
$`R_{\mathrm{task}}`$ as the normalized game score, which provides a
dense, comparable measure of progress across trajectories
($`\mathrm{max\_score}=350`$ for Zork I). We use this environment for
the Jericho Zork1 RL experiments, training the models to condition its
behavior on different time budgets and to trade off exploration, task
progress, and budget adherence.

##### MLE-Bench.

Prompting alone produced weak adherence to the specified time budget.
Without direct access to wall-clock time, models cannot reliably
estimate how long previous actions, tool calls, or reasoning steps have
taken. A model could in principle track time itself by querying a system
clock, but we did not observe this. The total wall-clock time consumed
was largely insensitive to the budget stated in the prompt: on MLE-Bench
with prompting only, the agent used 161 percent of a 15-minute budget on
average, and only 15 percent of runs finished within the stated limit
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).

##### Zork I.

Figure 2: Zork1 performance and time expenditure for Qwen3-4B with
thinking mode disabled under per-episode time budgets, in four
fixed-weight prompting conditions and two policies trained for 400 GRPO
steps against the budget ($`n=16`$ episodes per cell; episodes are
terminated at $`2\times`$ the budget, which serves as a hard cutoff).
(a) Mean score against budget: the trained policies attain 46.4 and 16.6
points at 16 s, whereas no fixed-weight condition exceeds 0.6 points at
any budget. (b) Elapsed time for the same episodes at budgets of 1, 4,
and 16 s, with one marker per episode and horizontal jitter; dashed gray
denotes the budget and dashed red the $`2\times`$ budget hard cutoff.
Stating the budget in the prompt alone does not meaningfully improve
adherence, while AutoClock is the most effective harness-based
intervention. RL yields the strongest overall performance, achieving
both the best budget adherence and substantially higher task scores.

Stating the time budget in the prompt alone does not lead to reliable
budget adherence. As shown by the Budget in Prompt rows in
Table [6](#Sx2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents"),
all models substantially overshoot the stated budget, often running
until the hard cutoff at $`2\times`$ the budget terminates the episode
(See Fig
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Zork I. ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents").b).
Task performance also remains near zero for most models. This behavior
is expected: the models have no direct notion of wall-clock generation
speed and receive no feedback about how much time has elapsed during
execution. As a result, a stated budget provides a constraint in natural
language, however out of the box models do not exhibit the ability to
apply the constraint.

### 4.2 Interventions via Harness

##### MLE-Bench.

Exposing elapsed time through the harness made the agent substantially
more responsive to its budget. Three hooks
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ MLE-Bench. ‣ 4.2 Interventions via Harness ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents"))
report the time remaining and the cost of generation, without
prescribing any action. This reduced the time consumed from $`161.4\%`$
to $`99.7\%`$ of the stated budget, with no measurable change in quality
($`47.5`$ to $`47.0`$ percentile, within error), and raised the fraction
of runs producing a valid submission from $`78\%`$ to $`88\%`$
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).

|                       |                             |                                                                                                       |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hook                  | When it fires               | What it does                                                                                          |
| Per-tool clock        | After every tool call       | Adds the time remaining to the result the agent reads                                                 |
| Periodic reminder     | On a fixed time interval    | Reports the time remaining even while a command is still running                                      |
| Generation accounting | After every tool call       | Reports how long the model spent generating text before the action                                    |
| Enforcement (clamp)   | Before a shell command runs | Shortens the command’s time limit so it stops by the deadline; the command still runs, but is cut off |
| Enforcement (refuse)  | Before a shell command runs | Blocks the command and returns a message explaining why, so the agent must choose something cheaper   |

Table 3: Harness hooks. The first three only add information to what the
agent reads. The two enforcement modes change the action itself and are
never used together.

The dominant failure mode was that when the agent recognized that little
time remained, it launched a tool call whose duration exceeded that
budget (for example a training with a timeout that is longer than the
time remaining). Because the duration of a tool call is variable and
hard to predict, the agent often had no further chance to act before it
ran past the budget. Even when prompted to put tool calls in the
background so it can interrupt the runs, the model is still unable to
consistently stop in time.

We therefore added an enforcement hook that inspects each shell command
before it runs, comparing the time limit the agent set for the command
against the time remaining. Because commands are frequently issued with
no limit, a missing limit is treated as the harness default timeout.
Enforcement cut the overrun further, at a small cost in quality. The
on-time rate improved, while quality fell slightly. The quality cost is
unsurprising, since the unenforced model was converting overrun time
into score, and enforcement takes that time away. Shortening a command’s
limit preserved most of the unenforced quality and produced the highest
rate of valid submissions we measured ($`90\%`$). Blocking commands
outright held closer to the budget but reduced the valid formatted
submission rate while increaseing interaction steps, because the agent
reissued blocked commands with smaller limits.

Even without RL training, the agent scales its elapsed time to the
stated budget when given a clock.
Figure [4](#Sx2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
(Appendix) shows the time and quality distributions across four budgets.
Quality is spread across the full percentile range at every budget, with
no upward trend as budget grows.

##### Zork I.

To provide agents with an explicit sense of elapsed time, we introduce
three harness-level interventions in Zork. First, the Clock Tool allows
the model to issue a time_elapsed tool call, which returns a message of
the form \[time used: $`x`$s of $`B`$s budget\]. Second, Clock Tool++
uses the same tool interface but provides substantially more guidance in
the prompt on when and how to query it, together with an in-context
example demonstrating its use. Third, the Auto-Clock harness removes the
need for the model to actively request timing information after every
interaction turn by having the harness automatically appends the same
elapsed-time message to the context.

The basic Clock Tool practically yields no improvements in adherence
(See Fig
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Zork I. ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
and Table
[6](#Sx2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).
Even though the model now has access to wall-clock time, it must still
decide when to query the tool, and models often fail to call it
frequently enough for the feedback to be useful. Consequently, most
models still continue to substantially overshoot short budgets. With
Clock Tool++, however, models invoke the tool much more often
(Table [8](#Sx2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
in Appendix), and the resulting increase in timing feedback leads to a
comparatively better budget adherence. The strongest adherence comes
from the Auto-Clock harness, where timing information is pushed into the
context after every turn rather than being requested by the model. Under
this intervention, most models track the available budget substantially
more closely. However, a limitation is that harness feedback is only
available between generations: if a single generation itself consumes a
large fraction of the budget, the harness cannot intervene until that
generation completes. This effect is particularly visible for larger
models such as 9B and 27B. Another interesting observation is that the
score remains below $`5`$ across all budgets, despite substantially
improved budget adherence. This suggests that access to time feedback
helps the model determine _when to stop_, but does not teach it _how to
adapt its strategy_. Therefore, we observe no meaningful score–budget
trade-off in the frontier shown in
Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Zork I. ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")(a).

### 4.3 Interventions via RL Training

#### 4.3.1 MLE-Bench

##### Objective.

We train with GRPO \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]. Let $`B`$ be the budget, $`t`$
the elapsed wall-clock time, and $`q\in[0,1]`$ the normalized task score
of the submission left behind. The reward is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
R(q,t)=\begin{cases}q+c_{\mathrm{time}},&\text{submitted and }t\leq B,\\[4.0pt]
\alpha\,q-p\,(t-B),&\text{submitted and }t>B,\\[4.0pt]
-\,c_{\mathrm{fail}},&\text{no submission},\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

with $`c_{\mathrm{time}}>0`$ as a bonus for finishing within the budget,
$`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ as the share of quality kept when late, $`p>0`$ as
the penalty per second of overrun, and $`c_{\mathrm{fail}}>0`$ as the
cost of producing nothing. The constants are set so that, at equal
quality, finishing on time always beats finishing late, and producing
nothing is always worst.

##### Results.

We show results on MLE-bench in
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents").
Training did not improve over the harness it was trained under. Training
did reduce interaction steps from $`20.3`$ to $`18.9`$, improving upon
the retry behavior that the enforcing plugin introduced.

The trained policy scaled its effort with the budget. The percent of
budget used regardless of the set budget held between $`0.87`$ and
$`0.93`$ in every run. On the other hand, about a quarter of on-time
submissions scored no better than a uniform guess, and this fraction did
not fall when the weight on $`q`$ (quality) was tripled. The GRPO
training was unable to improve the models ability to perform on the
subset of MLEBench tasks, but did enforce its ability to stay on budget.

#### 4.3.2 Zork I

##### Objective.

Let $`B`$ be the budget in seconds, stated verbatim in the prompt (see
[Prompts](#Sx2.SSx5 "In Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")),
$`t`$ the wall-clock time the episode consumed, and
$`s=\mathrm{score}/\mathrm{score}_{\max}\in[0,1]`$ the normalized game
score the agent holds when the episode ends
($`\mathrm{score}_{\max}=350`$ for Zork I). The game score is read off
the live game directly. The reward must supply a reason to *stop*, since
the agent may end the episode itself with quit and otherwise plays until
a hard $`180`$ s wall-clock kill or the turn cap. Below, we describe the
reward functions we explore. All reward functions share the following
form:

|     |                                                           |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(s,t)\;=\;\bigl[\,s+\lambda\,b(t;B)\,\bigr]\cdot g(t;B),
       ```                                                        |     | (2) |

with $`b\in[0,1]`$ as a time bonus, $`g\in\{0,1\}`$ as a gate that voids
the whole reward, and $`\lambda>0`$ weighting time against score (the
score always carries weight $`1`$; we use $`\lambda=0.1`$). The four
schemes, detailed in
Table [10](#Sx2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
(Appendix), differ only in $`b`$ and $`g`$. (i) *Cutoff* is a pure gate
with no bonus (ii) *Linear* and (iii) *Gaussian* are smooth peaks at
$`t=B`$ that pay for arriving near the budget from either side (iv)
*Step* is a coarse ramp that pays for elapsed time in tenths of $`B`$
and then voids the episode past $`1.1B`$. We select the step-wise reward
for training our RL models. Although the shaped rewards exhibit broadly
comparable behavior, step-wise provides the best overall balance between
convergence speed, task score, and budget adherence
(Table [7](#Sx2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).
We train the RL policies by sampling a time budget uniformly from 0 to
16s at each GRPO step and optimizing with the step-wise reward. We apply
this training procedure to both the AutoClock and Clock Tool++
interventions and referring the resulting runs as RL + AutoClock and
RL + Clock Tool++, respectively. In both settings, the policies learn to
remain within the allotted budget while also improving task performance
under that budget and pushing the frontier (See Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Zork I. ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")(a)).
However, RL + Clock Tool++ underperforms RL + AutoClock in score
(Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Zork I. ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
and
Table [6](#Sx2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).
We attribute this gap to the overhead of active time checking since RL +
Clock Tool++ spends roughly 50% of its turns querying the clock, leaving
fewer actions for task progress. Despite this inefficiency, both
policies achieve strong adherence, with generations typically
terminating within $`\pm 15\%`$ of the specified budget.

Clock generalizes, the play doesn’t: We also train the same policy using
discrete budgets rather than sampling uniformly from a continuous range,
which allows us to study substantially longer horizons such as 15, 30,
60, and 90,s. Each rollout is assigned a budget from a predefined set we
call budget mix, and the corresponding budget is provided to the model
in the prompt. In principle, interleaving multiple budgets during
training should encourage the policy to condition its behavior on the
available time and use larger budgets for more extensive exploration. As
training progresses, budget adherence becomes nearly perfect across the
different horizons. However, the policy collapses toward the strategy
learned for the smallest budget
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Objective. ‣ 4.3.2 Zork I ‣ 4.3 Interventions via RL Training ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")).
Trajectories for different budgets separate cleanly in elapsed
wall-clock time but their game scores follow nearly identical trends
throughout training. Thus, the model learns *when to stop* for each
requested budget, but not *how to use additional time productively* to
improve task performance.

(a) Budget mix $`\{15,30,60,90\}`$.

(b) Budget mix $`\{15,90\}`$.

## 5 Limitations

Strategy collapse across budgets: The trained policy learns to closely
follow itself to the stated budget but does not plan differently for it.
In Zork, rollouts under different budgets open with the same memorized
action sequence and reach the same score regardless of budget given. The
budget changes only how long the episode is padded with filler actions
before the agent quits. Mixed-budget training was intended to prevent
this collapse, and it succeeded only at helping the model generalize
stopping to multiple budgets. The same pattern holds on MLE-Bench, where
extra time bought more attempts training models, but did not improve the
final score. Also see [Budget adherence through invalid
actions](#Sx1.SSx2 "In Appendix ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents").

Memorization in fixed environments: Training on a single game with a
fixed starting state makes memorization the cheapest path to higher
score. The Zork policy converges on a recalled walkthrough prefix that
collects a fixed number of points, after which no new score is found.
When valid actions are fed back to the model instead of its own outputs,
the same checkpoint scores far lower, confirming that the learned
behavior does not survive even a small change. The reward structure
compounds this problem by pricing elapsed time and not exploration, so
once a scoring prefix exists, deviating from it offers no benefit. It
also does not distinguish a rejected action from a productive one, and
the trained policy fills remaining time by repeating a command. Budget
utilization therefore only demonstrates the ability of the model to stop
on time, but not on how well it used the allotted time. We discuss these
mechanisms, and a third source of noise from stochastic action durations
on MLE-Bench, in the Appendix.

Scope of evaluation: Our experiments use two models (Qwen3-4B and
Qwen3.6-27B) and two environments, and the RL experiments on Zork train
on a single game. Whether the findings extend to frontier-scale models,
to environments with richer strategy spaces remains open. The MLE-Bench
subset contains five competitions, which limits the diversity of task
structures the policy encounters during training. A broader evaluation
across models, environment types, and task counts would strengthen the
conclusions drawn here.

## 6 Conclusion

We studied whether LLM agents can reason about and act under explicit
time budgets, comparing two classes of interventions: (i) harness-based
mechanisms that expose or enforce time information, and (ii) GRPO
training that directly optimizes budget-conditioned behavior. Simply
stating a time budget in the prompt is not sufficient: out-of-the-box
agents struggle to estimate action durations, overshooting small budgets
by up to $`2\times`$ on Zork and by $`61\%`$ on MLE-Bench. In contrast,
exposing time through the agent harness substantially improves
adherence. Informational clocks reduce overruns to near zero in both
environments with little measurable loss in task quality, while stricter
enforcement hooks tighten adherence further at a modest performance
cost.

GRPO training improves budget adherence further. On Zork, the trained
policy matches the requested budget to within $`0.2`$ s across budgets
from $`5`$ to $`90`$ s, including four held-out budgets not seen during
training. On MLE-Bench, trained policies consistently use between
$`0.87`$ and $`0.93`$ of the allocated budget. At smaller budgets, RL
also pushes the cost–score frontier outward, improving both adherence
and task performance. However, this improvement does not extend
uniformly to larger budgets. In these sparse-reward regimes, the current
objectives provide little incentive for deeper exploration or
qualitatively different strategies. On Zork, the policy converges to a
fixed high-reward prefix and spends additional time on unproductive
actions, causing score to saturate at $`45/350`$ across larger budgets.
Similarly on MLE-Bench, additional time similarly leads to more attempts
at essentially the same training procedure without improving submission
quality.

We show that these results reveal a distinction between *budget
adherence* and *productive budget allocation* (ability to change its
behavior when given more time). These findings should be interpreted in
light of three limitations: strategy collapse across budgets,
memorization induced by fixed training environments and sparse rewards,
and the limited scope of our evaluation across models and tasks.
Possible directions include exploration-aware rewards that pay for novel
states rather than elapsed time, environment variation that prevents
memorization from substituting for search, and reward terms that
distinguish repeated attempts from genuinely different strategies. The
gap between adherence (which RL solves) and productive time allocation
(which remains open) defines the central challenge for
budget-conditioned agents.

## Appendix

### Reward structure and exploration incentives

The reward is a function of final score and elapsed time only, so
exploring is unpriced. In Zork, once a scoring prefix exists, deviation
is actively risky. Our 4B models typically reach at most about
$`45/350\approx 0.129`$ in score. With $`\lambda=0.1`$, the time term is
worth up to $`0.100`$, which is already comparable to the score term
achieved by the policy. Moreover, because Zork rewards are relatively
discrete, a meaningful improvement often requires gaining several
additional points; gaining five more points, for example, increases the
score term by only $`5/350\approx 0.014`$. Perfect budget adherence is
therefore worth about seven times as much as a genuine five-point
discovery, and it is available deterministically from any token sequence
that consumes the clock. Fixing this would require a term that pays for
novelty (first-visit bonuses, walkthrough coverage, or potential-based
shaping on distance to unreached states), together with environment
variation across episodes so that recall cannot substitute for search.

On MLE-Bench, the analogous problem is that the reward does not
distinguish between repeated attempts at the same strategy and genuinely
different approaches. A policy that submits the same baseline three
times under a longer budget receives the same reward as one that tries
progressively more sophisticated methods, as long as the best submission
score is identical.

### Budget adherence through invalid actions

Because the Zork time term is satisfied by wall-clock alone, the policy
learns to consume the clock by emitting commands the parser rejects. In
one particular training at step 500 the filler is the word forward, to
which Zork replies I don’t know the word "forward". It appears in
$`127`$ of $`128`$ rollouts, immediately after the memorized prefix
ends, and accounts for $`45\%`$ of turns at $`B=15`$ and $`88\%`$ of
turns at $`B=90`$. The budget is met to within $`0.2`$ s almost entirely
through repetition of an action that advances nothing, since elapsed
time measures wall-clock latency regardless of whether the action was
accepted, and a rejected command consumes the same generation time as a
valid move.

This means “used $`99\%`$ of its budget” should not be read as $`99\%`$
of the budget spent working. Any claim about effort allocation requires
a measure of useful time (turns that change game state, valid-command
rate, or tokens spent on accepted actions). This failure mode is also
easy to miss with the wrong diagnostic. Our repetition detector reports
a trailing identical run of only $`1.0`$–$`1.5`$ turns for these runs,
because it measures the tail identical to the *final* action (quit), so
hundreds of consecutive no-ops sit outside its window. Penalizing
invalid actions or crediting only state-changing turns is a prerequisite
for interpreting time-shaped rewards as effort.

### Comparing Reward Shapes

Across the shaped variants, *linear*, *Gaussian*, and *step* perform
comparably overall, suggesting that the precise shape of the time reward
matters little once an explicit timing signal is present. The main
difference is in budget matching. The *step* reward produces the most
reliable adherence to the target budget, since it does not reward the
model at all for being over budget. A more detailed comparison of the
reward shapes and their resulting behavior is provided in
Table [10](#Sx2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
(Appendix).

### Action durations on MLE-Bench

On MLE-Bench, action durations are stochastic and depend on factors
outside the agent’s control (GPU availability, data loading, network
latency). The same training script may take $`30`$ seconds or $`3`$
minutes depending on system load. This makes the reward noisy in a way
that is uncorrelated with the agent’s decisions, complicating credit
assignment during RL \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. The harness-only condition
already achieves $`99.7\%`$ budget utilization, leaving little room for
RL to improve, and the variance in action duration may explain why RL
training on MLE-Bench produced negligible gains over the untrained
harness.

## Implementation Details

### Environment and Interaction Protocol

Each turn the model receives the game’s response, a status line \[score:
$`s`$/350 \| moves: $`m`$\], and the fixed question What is your next
action?. It must reply with exactly two lines, a REASONING: line and an
ACTION: line (the full template is in the base system prompt, reproduced
under *Prompts* below). Parsing takes the last line beginning with
ACTION:; failing that, the last non-empty line; failing that, the
fallback command look. The extracted command is stripped of surrounding
quotes and backticks and truncated to $`190`$ characters (Jericho
truncates commands at $`198`$ bytes). A truncated generation therefore
never aborts an episode: it silently degrades to look, and the rate of
such turns is recorded per configuration.

An episode terminates on any of: the agent emitting ACTION: quit (the
prompt requires this, so voluntary termination is the intended exit),
game over or victory, max_turns $`=4000`$, the wall-clock cutoff defined
below, a server-side context-length overflow (recorded separately as
context_limit), or an LLM error. The end reason is recorded for every
episode; the split between *agent quit* and *harness cutoff* is one of
the primary dependent variables, since it identifies who actually
enforced the deadline.

In the benchmark harness the message history is trimmed to the most
recent $`100`$ turn-pairs, always retaining the system prompt and the
opening observation and always resuming on an assistant message. At the
cutoffs used here ($`\leq 80`$ s) no episode reaches $`100`$ turns, so
the trimming is a no-op; it is kept so that longer budgets cannot
silently measure context exhaustion instead of play (an untrimmed
episode dies on the context limit at roughly turn $`250`$, worst for
Qwen3-4B, whose native context is $`40{,}960`$ tokens).

### Time Budget, Cutoff, and the Definition of Elapsed Time

Every timed episode is given a budget $`B`$ seconds and is killed by the
harness at a cutoff of $`2B`$. Elapsed time is wall clock measured from
the start of the episode; it includes generation latency, environment
stepping and all overhead, and it is exactly the quantity the model is
shown or can query. Two properties of the cutoff matter for interpreting
results, and both are shared by the benchmark and the training loop by
construction:

- •
  The cutoff is checked before each generation and cannot interrupt one.
  Every episode therefore receives at least one generation, and elapsed
  time can exceed the cutoff. At a $`32`$ s cutoff this is a rounding
  error; at a $`1`$ s cutoff the single generation *is* the episode. We
  report $`\mathrm{overrun}=\text{elapsed}/\text{cutoff}`$ per
  configuration and mark any cell with $`\mathrm{overrun}\geq 1.5`$ as
  one in which the cutoff never bound, so that its score is not read as
  timed play. Note that this ratio is against the cutoff, not the
  budget: because the cutoff is $`2B`$, an episode that never stops
  voluntarily scores $`\approx 2.0\times`$ the budget, which is the
  ceiling rather than a pathology.
- •
  Sub-second budgets are below the latency of a single turn. One
  generation costs $`\approx 0.2`$–$`0.4`$ s for the 4B model at 16-way
  concurrency and $`1.4`$–$`1.8`$ s for the 27B; the fastest complete
  episode observed anywhere is $`0.233`$ s. Zork I’s first point is
  $`\approx 12`$ moves in. Budgets below $`\approx 2`$ s are
  consequently at the score floor by construction, and we use them only
  to measure clock behaviour (tool calls, quit rate, elapsed time),
  never as score conditions.

Elapsed time is rendered to the model at a precision the budget can
resolve: whole seconds for $`B\geq 10`$ s, one decimal for
$`1\leq B<10`$ s, two decimals below $`1`$ s. Without this, a $`0.5`$ s
budget would render every turn as \[time used: 0s of 0s budget\] and
erase the quantity under study.

### The Clock Interventions

The four interventions differ *only* in how the time budget reaches the
model. All four state the same budget in the system prompt and use the
same $`2B`$ cutoff, the same game, the same seeds and the same sampling
parameters.
Table [4](#Sx2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ The Clock Interventions ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
summarises them; the exact prompt text of each is given under *Prompts*
at the end of this section. A fifth condition, *No Budget*, states
nothing about time and serves as the control.

| Condition        | Budget in | Per-turn | Callable | System prompt   |
|------------------|-----------|----------|----------|-----------------|
|                  | prompt    | clock    | clock    | at $`B{=}16`$ s |
| No Budget        | –         | –        | –        | 1301            |
| Budget in Prompt | yes       | –        | –        | 1456            |
| Clock Tool       | yes       | –        | yes      | 1766            |
| Clock Tool++     | yes       | –        | yes      | 3013            |
| Auto-Clock       | yes       | yes      | –        | 1456            |

Table 4: The clock conditions. *Per-turn clock* appends \[time used:
$`x`$s of $`B`$s budget\] to every observation; *callable clock* lets
the model spend a turn on ACTION: time_elapsed to obtain the same
string. *Clock Tool* and *Clock Tool++* expose the identical tool and
return the identical reply, and differ only in how it is documented.
*Budget in Prompt* and *Auto-Clock* send the identical system prompt and
differ only in the user turns. The last column is the system-prompt
length in characters.

##### The clock tool is a text-protocol pseudo-tool, not native function calling.

The model requests the clock by replying ACTION: time_elapsed in place
of a game command, and receives the elapsed/budget line back without the
game advancing: no move is consumed, the score is untouched, and the
game state is unchanged. The only cost is the real time the generation
itself took, which is charged to the same budget. This was chosen over
OpenAI-style tools=\[…\] deliberately: native tool calling would route
the three model families through different vLLM tool-call parsers and a
different chat-template branch than the non-tool conditions use, adding
a confound to the single comparison the experiment exists to make. The
cost of the choice is that the condition measures whether a model
*chooses to check the clock*, not whether it can emit a tool-call
schema.

### Reinforcement Learning

##### Algorithm and loop.

We train with GRPO in verl, using a custom agent loop that plays Jericho
inside the rollout worker. Generated tokens carry
$`\texttt{response\_mask}=1`$; game observations, the clock-tool replies
and every other environment-authored user turn carry $`0`$ and are
excluded from the policy-gradient loss. The loop is registered as the
default agent loop and Jericho is stepped through an executor, so the
synchronous environment does not block the asynchronous rollout. The
trajectory reward is computed by the loop at episode end and returned
directly, bypassing the reward manager.

##### Reward.

With $`s`$ the normalised game score (score$`/350`$), $`t`$ the
episode’s elapsed wall clock and $`B`$ its budget, the reward is

|     |                                                        |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R=s+\lambda\cdot\mathrm{bonus}(t,B),\qquad\lambda=0.1,
       ```                                                     |     | (3) |

with the *step-wise* bonus used in every run reported here:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{bonus}(t,B)=\begin{cases}\min\!\left(1,\;\tfrac{1}{10}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{t}{0.1B}\right\rfloor+1\right)\right)&t\leq 1.1B,\\[4.0pt]
0\quad\text{and }R:=0&t>1.1B.\end{cases}
``` |  | (4) |

The bonus rises in ten steps of $`0.1`$ across the budget, saturates at
$`1.0`$ on the $`0.2B`$-wide plateau $`[0.9B,1.1B]`$ — the $`+1`$ in the
tenth index means the plateau begins at $`0.9B`$, not at $`B`$ — and
past $`1.1B`$ the *entire* reward including the score term is gated to
zero. Two consequences matter for reading the results. The risk is
asymmetric: overshooting costs every point in the game while
undershooting costs only partial credit. And because the plateau is wide
and everything outside it is gated, the mean bonus over a set of
trajectories is in practice a *pass rate* for “landed in
$`[0.9B,1.1B]`$” rather than a graded distance from $`B`$; we therefore
report $`t/B`$ alongside it, which is continuous and is recorded even
for gated episodes. Three further schemes are implemented and available
but not used in the reported runs: a linear tent ($`0`$ at $`t=0`$,
$`1`$ at $`t=B`$, $`0`$ at $`t\geq 2B`$), a Gaussian centred on $`B`$
with $`\sigma=10`$ s, and a hard gate ($`s`$ if $`t\leq B`$, else
$`0`$).

##### Hyperparameters.

Table [5](#Sx2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Hyperparameters. ‣ Reinforcement Learning ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")

the runs stay comparable.

|----|----|

| Policy | Qwen3-4B, trained from the base model (no warm start) |
| Learning rate | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ |
| Batching | train batch $`16`$, PPO mini-batch $`16`$, micro-batch $`1`$ per GPU, |
|  | gradient checkpointing on |
| Group size | $`n=8`$ rollouts per prompt $`\Rightarrow 128`$ episodes per step |
| Sampling | temperature $`1.0`$, thinking disabled |
| Context | prompt $`\leq 4096`$, response $`\leq 32768`$, max_model_len $`40960`$ |
|  | (Qwen3-4B native; no RoPE scaling) |
| Episode | max_turns $`4000`$, max_assistant_turns $`4000`$, |
|  | max_action_tokens $`2048`$, kill $`=2\times B`$ |

## Implementation Details: MLE-Bench

### Agent, Model Serving, and Sandbox

The agent is OpenCode 1.17.4, run headless (opencode run --format json)
with tool calls auto-approved. It uses OpenCode’s built-in tools (bash,
read, write, edit, glob, grep) and OpenCode’s own system prompt; the
task, paths, and budget are the first user message (reproduced under
*Prompts*). The agent is never given a clock it can call. In every
condition it either reads the clock lines the harness appends to tool
results or has no clock.

Qwen3.6-27B is served by SGLang with tensor parallelism $`4`$ and a
$`131{,}072`$-token context. OpenCode is configured with the same
context limit and an output limit of $`16{,}384`$ tokens per generation,
and compacts its history as it nears the limit. A proxy between OpenCode
and the inference server records the token ids and log-probabilities of
every generation in an episode, with a loss mask that is $`1`$ on
model-generated tokens and $`0`$ on everything the environment authored,
including tool results and the clock lines inside them. These records
are the training data.

Each episode runs in its own Docker container with one dedicated NVIDIA
GPU, one episode per container at a time, in a fresh workspace that is
deleted afterwards. The competition’s public files are linked into the
workspace read-only. The private test labels sit on the same read-only
mount and are read by the grader; the prompt tells the agent not to read
them, and nothing else prevents it. After every episode, all processes
it started are killed before grading, so a background job cannot change
submission.csv after the deadline or slow the next episode.

### Episode, Budget, and Elapsed Time

An episode is one OpenCode invocation. It ends when the agent exits or
when the harness kills it. In the
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
conditions the kill is at $`2B`$ ($`1800`$ s for the $`15`$-minute
budget); the RL run later moved it to $`B+30`$ s (see *Reinforcement
Learning*). whatever submission.csv is on disk at that moment is graded.

Elapsed time $`t`$ is wall clock from the moment the workspace is ready
to the moment the agent exits or is killed. It includes generation, tool
execution, and harness overhead, and it is the quantity the clock hooks
display. The start time is stored in a root-owned file the agent cannot
write. The reward takes the larger of the container’s reading and the
generator’s own clock, and a failed reading resolves to the cutoff
rather than to zero, so no failure can grade as an on-time finish.

*On budget* means $`t\leq B`$. *Turns* is the number of assistant steps
in the trajectory, one step being one generation. *Valid* is the
fraction of episodes whose file grades as a valid submission.

### Grading and Quality

After the episode, mlebench.grade.grade_csv grades submission.csv
against the private test labels inside the container and returns whether
the file is a valid submission (ids, columns, row count, no missing
values) and the competition metric. All competitions in the tables are
lower-is-better: multi-class log-loss for dog-breed identification,
spooky-author identification, and leaf classification; log-loss for
dogs-vs-cats; mean column-wise RMSLE for NOMAD 2018.

*Quality* is the leaderboard percentile: the percentage of entries on
the competition’s Kaggle leaderboard, as distributed with MLE-Bench,
that the episode’s score beats, ties counted as half. It is a monotone
transform of the metric and puts the competitions on one scale.

### Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents") and Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents") (left)

The budget-in-prompt runs on dog-breed identification predate the
harness above. They were made with an earlier launcher around the same
OpenCode agent and model, with no plugins, no resume loop, and no kill:
an episode ended when the agent exited. Each budget has its own prompt
file; the four files share one body of operating instructions and differ
only in the budget sentences reproduced under *Prompts*. The no-budget
prompt omits the time sentences entirely.

### Reinforcement Learning

##### Reward.

The reward in
Section [4.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS1 "4.3.1 MLE-Bench ‣ 4.3 Interventions via RL Training ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
is a simplified statement of the function the trainer received. Let
$`x=t/B`$ and $`L`$ the graded metric. The quality term is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q=c_{q}\cdot\frac{L_{\mathrm{bad}}-L}{L_{\mathrm{bad}}-L_{\mathrm{good}}},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`L_{\mathrm{bad}}`$ is the competition’s uniform-guess metric
($`\ln`$ of the number of classes for the log-loss tasks; the 90th
percentile of observed scores for NOMAD, which has no analytic chance
level) and $`L_{\mathrm{good}}`$ is the 5th percentile of scores
observed in earlier runs. Chance scores $`q=0`$, so a copy of
sample_submission.csv or a constant prediction, which grades as valid,
earns no quality credit. The 5th-percentile score earns $`q=c_{q}`$.
Below chance the slope is one fifth of the in-band slope and $`q`$ is
floored at $`-1.5`$, so miscalibrated submissions stay ordered but one
outlier cannot dominate a group; above $`L_{\mathrm{good}}`$ the line
continues unchanged. Let $`Q=q+c_{\mathrm{sub}}`$, with
$`c_{\mathrm{sub}}`$ a flat bonus for any gradeable file. Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R=\begin{cases}Q+c_{\mathrm{time}}+s\,Q\,(1-x),&\text{valid and }t\leq B,\\[3.0pt]
\kappa\,Q-p_{\max}\bigl(1-e^{-(t-B)/\tau}\bigr),&\text{valid
and }t>B,\\[3.0pt]
-\,c_{\mathrm{fail}}-k\,x,&\text{no valid submission.}\end{cases}
``` |  | (6) |

The speed term is scaled by $`Q`$ so a poor model submitted quickly does
not out-score a good model on time. The late penalty is strictly
decreasing in lateness, with no flat region, and bounded by $`p_{\max}`$
so the worst late valid submission still beats the best invalid one. The
invalid penalty grows with $`x`$ so running to the cutoff with no file
is worse than exiting early with no file.
Table [11](#Sx3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Reward. ‣ Reinforcement Learning ‣ Implementation Details: MLE-Bench ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
lists the constants. With the final set, the worst on-time valid reward
exceeds the best late valid reward on every competition, which we check
before each run.

| Symbol | Meaning | Steps 1–105 | Steps 106–182 |
|----|----|----|----|
| $`q`$ | quality term | $`1/(1+L)`$ | band, $`c_{q}=3.0`$ |
| $`c_{\mathrm{sub}}`$ | bonus for a gradeable file | $`0.25`$ | $`0.25`$ |
| $`c_{\mathrm{time}}`$ | bonus for finishing on budget | $`1.0`$ | $`0.5`$ |
| $`s`$ | on-budget speed slope | $`0.5`$ | $`0.15`$ |
| $`\kappa`$ | share of $`Q`$ kept when late | $`0.3`$ | $`0.8`$ |
| $`p_{\max}`$ | maximum late penalty | $`1.35`$ | $`1.35`$ |
| $`\tau`$ | late-penalty time constant | $`200`$ s | $`20`$ s |
| $`c_{\mathrm{fail}}`$ | penalty for no valid submission | $`1.5`$ | $`3.0`$ |
| $`k`$ | slope of the invalid penalty in $`x`$ | $`1.5`$ | $`1.5`$ |

Table 11: Reward constants for the MLE-Bench GRPO run. The run launched
with the left column and the compressive quality map $`1/(1+L)`$; the
band and the right column replaced them at step $`106`$, after the kill
moved to $`B+30`$ s and lateness no longer had to be priced. The RL row
of
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Prompting ‣ 4 Results ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
is from the second phase.

##### Groups and budgets.

One GRPO group is one (competition, budget) pair, so advantages are
computed among episodes told the same deadline. The budget in the
prompt, the budget the plugins display, the kill, and every reward
branch are set from the same per-group value. The run sweeps $`5`$
competitions $`\times`$ $`4`$ budgets ($`10,15,20,25`$ minutes): $`20`$
groups of $`21`$ episodes, $`420`$ episodes per optimizer step, one step
per sweep. Dogs-vs-cats is the fifth competition, included so that every
step has $`20`$ groups, and is excluded from the tables. All episodes in
a step are generated on one weight version, and the trainer applies
truncated importance sampling to the recorded log-probabilities to
correct the staleness between generation and update.
Table [12](#Sx3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Groups and budgets. ‣ Reinforcement Learning ‣ Implementation Details: MLE-Bench ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
lists the remaining settings.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Algorithm | GRPO, KL loss on (low-variance estimator), coefficient $`0.001`$ |
| Policy | Qwen3.6-27B, trained from the released weights |
| Learning rate | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$, constant; weight decay $`0.1`$ |
| Group size | $`21`$ episodes per (competition, budget); $`20`$ groups per step |
| Response length | $`\leq 16{,}384`$ tokens per generation |
| Parallelism | tensor parallel $`4`$, pipeline parallel $`2`$ |
| Checkpoints | every $`25`$ steps |

Table 12: GRPO configuration for MLE-Bench.

### Time-Estimation Probes

The probes behind
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
(right) and
Table [9](#Sx2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Prompts ‣ Implementation Details ‣ On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents")
reuse recorded $`15`$-minute episodes. A trajectory is truncated
mid-episode, the model is asked how much time has elapsed, how much
budget remains, how much longer the run will take, and what the total
duration will be, and its answers are compared with the recorded values.
The clock condition is set by keeping or removing the harness clock
lines from the truncated context; the episodes are the same in both
conditions. Responses that continue issuing tool calls instead of
answering are dropped.

and the RL run send the task prompt below as the first user message,
with the competition slug, data path, workspace path, submission path,
and budget in minutes filled in per episode. Paragraphs are wrapped for
display; the string has newlines at paragraph boundaries and between
bullets.

The
````
